title: Lumenary ME
subtitle: Mechanical engineering from simple machines to the design, energy and manufacturing systems of 2026: mechanics, solids, thermodynamics and fluids, design and manufacturing, dynamics and control, energy, and the frontier.
description: Lumenary ME is the mechanical-engineering subject of Lumenary Scientia, free and open source like the others. It starts with no experience at all — forces, levers and gears — and climbs through statics and dynamics, the mechanics of materials and the finite element method, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics and heat transfer, machine design and manufacturing, system dynamics and mechatronics, and energy systems, to the simulation-driven design, advanced manufacturing and engineering for computing, energy and space of 2026.

Every lesson teaches with ideas first and calculation second. Calculations and simulations — truss forces, beam deflections, vibrations, thermodynamic cycles, pipe flow, heat conduction, a small finite element solver — are in Python with NumPy, and every block with a **Run in browser** button runs there, with nothing to install. A lesson says *Code tested* only when all of its code passed. Lumenary ME shares ground with [Lumenary EE](/en/ee/) (motors and control), [Lumenary Robotics](/en/robotics/) and [Lumenary Materials](/en/materials/), and links to them where they meet.

Machines and tools can hurt you. Lessons that involve making anything say what is safe to try — cardboard, wood and plastic models, hand tools used with care and supervision, 3D printers used as their makers intend — and why workshops have guards, protective equipment and training.

Every lesson was drafted with AI assistance and is awaiting review by a human mechanical engineer. The text, exercises and code are original and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (code Apache-2.0). Where a standards body, manufacturer, laboratory or open-source project has published the primary source, the lesson links to it rather than retelling it.

ui.awaitingReview: Awaiting review by a mechanical engineer

levels.title: Forces and machines
levels.summary: No experience needed, from about age 11. Forces and motion, simple machines, energy and efficiency, why structures stand up, and how things are made — safely.

levels.title: Engineering mechanics
levels.summary: Forces in balance and in motion: statics and free-body diagrams, trusses and frames, the dynamics of particles and rigid bodies, and vibrations.

levels.title: Mechanics of materials
levels.summary: How parts carry load and how they fail: stress and strain, axial load, torsion and bending, deflection and buckling, failure and fatigue, and the finite element method.

levels.title: Thermodynamics, fluids and heat
levels.summary: Energy, flow and heat: the first and second laws, power and refrigeration cycles, fluid statics and Bernoulli, viscous flow in pipes, heat transfer, and computational fluid dynamics.

levels.title: Design and manufacturing
levels.summary: From an idea to a part in your hand: the engineering design process and CAD, machine elements, mechanisms and linkages, manufacturing processes, and additive manufacturing.

levels.title: Dynamics, control and mechatronics
levels.summary: Machines as systems: modelling mechanical, thermal and fluid systems, controlling them, mechatronics and actuators, and vehicles and propulsion.

levels.title: Energy systems
levels.summary: The machines that convert energy: power plants and energy conversion, wind and water turbines, and heating, cooling and buildings.

levels.title: The frontier of mechanical engineering
levels.summary: Where the field is moving in 2026, with links to the primary sources: simulation-driven and generative design, advanced manufacturing, cooling for computing, sustainable engineering, and engineering for space and fusion.
